title: Even Devadatta
hook: in the Lotus Sutra he too is promised Buddhahood, a Mahayana view (Lotus Sutra, Devadatta chapter)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devadatta's plots: hired men, a rock, an elephant, and a split. Your line was the split. Today, how his story ends, and a chapter that goes further.

What happens to Devadatta in the end? The Pali commentaries tell it starkly. Late in life, tradition says, he set out to see the Buddha and ask forgiveness, and the earth opened and swallowed him before he arrived. The same commentaries add a quieter line: far in the future, even he will come to awakening. And a Mahayana scripture, the Lotus Sutra, has a chapter that carries his name and goes further still. It doesn't begin with Devadatta's crimes. It begins with a king, long ago, who wanted to learn.
screen: `THE EARTH OPENS.` → `A DOOR LEFT OPEN.` → `A CHAPTER WITH HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the king. In the chapter, the Buddha tells of a past life when he was a king who wanted the highest teaching so much that he was ready to give up his throne for it. He would serve anyone who could teach him. Second, the seer. A seer came who knew a sutra, the Lotus, and would teach it if the king became his servant. So the king picked fruit, drew water, gathered firewood, prepared food, even let his own body be the seer's seat, and never wearied of it. Third, the name. That seer, the Buddha says, was Devadatta. Because of Devadatta, his good friend, he came to complete the qualities of a buddha. Fourth, the promise. After a vast stretch of time, the chapter says, Devadatta himself will become a buddha, named Heavenly King. This is a Mahayana view, and it's fair to say plainly whose it is. Theravada Buddhists read the Pali Vinaya and commentaries, where Devadatta's deeds bring heavy results, though the commentaries also leave that far door open. In some Mahayana schools, the Lotus chapter is read as saying no one stands outside the reach of awakening, not even the cousin who rolled the rock. Some teachers also read it about enemies: the one who opposed you may turn out, in a long enough view, to be part of what formed you. Neither tradition says what Devadatta did was small. Both keep the warning. The Lotus chapter sets a promise beside it.
screen: `A KING WHO WANTED THE TEACHING.` · `A SEER WHO TAUGHT HIM.` · `THAT SEER WAS DEVADATTA.` · `HE TOO WILL BE A BUDDHA.` · then, large: `EVEN HIM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has opposed you, not the worst, someone in the middle: a rival, a critic, someone who made one season harder. If you practice loving-kindness, use the phrases it already uses; if not, simply wish them one good thing, a good night's sleep or a kind word. Wishing them well doesn't approve of what they did, just as the Lotus chapter doesn't excuse Devadatta.
Even Devadatta. In the Lotus Sutra, the cousin who split the sangha is named the Buddha's past teacher and promised buddhahood. Today's word.
Your line: even him. The warning stays, and a far door is left open. Day seven hundred seventy-eight, done.

howItsDone: In some Mahayana communities the Lotus Sutra is chanted and studied, and its Devadatta chapter is read as a teaching that awakening reaches everyone; in Theravada communities Devadatta's story is told from the Pali Vinaya and commentaries as a warning about envy and ambition.

chat.says: Does the Lotus Sutra say what Devadatta did was okay?
options: No. It keeps the warning, but says even he will one day be a buddha.
Yes. It says the rock and the split were never really wrong.
No. It says that after the split he can never awaken at all.
chat.meaning: Neither tradition calls Devadatta's deeds small. The Lotus chapter keeps the warning and sets a promise beside it: he too will become a buddha.

Lotus Sutra.meaning: a Mahayana scripture with a chapter named for Devadatta

Mahayana.meaning: the 'great vehicle', one broad family of Buddhist schools

Theravada.meaning: the 'way of the elders', which reads the Pali canon

Heavenly King.meaning: Devadatta's future name as a buddha, in the Lotus chapter

Vinaya.meaning: the monastic discipline; its texts tell Devadatta's story

notes: The Devadatta chapter is a separate chapter (ch. 12) in Kumarajiva's Chinese version; in some Sanskrit versions the material sits within the Stupa chapter. The script cites only 'the Devadatta chapter', as the index does.
Confirm details of the king's service as paraphrased (fruit, water, firewood, food, his body as the seer's seat, never wearying) and the seer's name, Asita, omitted here.
Confirm the future buddha name 'Heavenly King' (Devaraja) and the phrase 'good friend' (kalyanamitra).

The Theravada account of Devadatta swallowed by the earth on his way to ask forgiveness, and his future awakening as the paccekabuddha Atthissara, is from the Dhammapada commentary (and Jataka commentary); confirm and confirm the fair phrasing 'leave that far door open'.
The reading about enemies ('part of what formed you') is attributed to 'some teachers'; confirm it is fair to Mahayana teaching on this chapter (e.g. Nichiren's reading).
The chapter's second episode, the naga king's daughter, is left out to keep one idea; consider for another day.
